stories.title: Trucks May Have Dumped Singapore's Rubbish in Malaysian Villages
stories.headline_kid: Malaysian officials are investigating nine companies accused of secretly dumping building rubbish from Singapore near villages across the border.
summary: Imagine finishing a big construction project and having piles of broken bricks, concrete and sand left over. This is called construction waste, and it must be thrown away properly and safely. But Johor's waste management agency says nine companies did something wrong with this kind of rubbish.

Officials allege the companies carried construction waste from Singapore across the Tuas Second Link, which is a bridge connecting Singapore to Johor, Malaysia. Instead of disposing of it properly, they allegedly dumped it near villages in an area called Pontian.

This matters because dumped waste can pollute soil, block waterways and even harm the health of people living nearby. It's a bit like sneaking your rubbish into your neighbour's garden instead of putting it in the proper bin.
Johor authorities have visited the dumping site and are now investigating the companies involved. If found guilty, the companies could face serious punishment for breaking environmental laws.

lenses.me: It shows why throwing rubbish in the right place matters, even for big companies, not just kids in school.
lenses.family: If your family renovates your home, this reminds us that construction waste must be disposed of properly, not dumped somewhere illegal.
lenses.friends: You and your friends can talk about why littering, even 'big' littering, affects real people and places.
lenses.nation: Singapore and Malaysia need to work together to solve problems that cross both countries' borders.
lenses.world: It shows that pollution doesn't stay in one place — waste from one country can affect people in another.

stories.title: Man Caught with Fake ID Passes and Stamps at Woodlands Checkpoint
stories.headline_kid: A 23-year-old man was caught with fake employee passes and stamps that copied real government seals, and he will be charged for it.
summary: A 23-year-old Malaysian man was stopped at Woodlands Checkpoint, the border crossing between Singapore and Malaysia. Officers found fake employee passes on him, along with stamps that looked official.

The stamps had designs copying the emblems of the Supreme Court and the Ministry of Home Affairs — like pretending to have a special school badge that you didn't actually earn. These items are linked to scams, which are tricks used to cheat people out of money.

Scammers sometimes pretend to be police officers, court officials or government workers to scare victims into believing they are in trouble, so the victims will hand over money out of fear. Fake passes and stamps help make these lies look convincing.

The man will be charged in court on Thursday. This case is a reminder that scammers can go to great lengths to trick people, so it's always wise to double-check before believing anyone claiming to represent the government.

lenses.me: It teaches you to be careful and question things that seem official but feel suspicious.
lenses.family: Your parents or grandparents might get scam calls pretending to be from the police — this case shows how real these tricks can look.
lenses.friends: You can share scam-safety tips with friends so everyone knows what to watch out for.
lenses.nation: Singapore takes scams seriously and works hard to catch people who create fake documents to cheat others.
lenses.world: Scams like this often involve people crossing borders, showing how crime doesn't stop at country lines.

stories.title: Another Singaporean Rescued from Kidnappers in Malaysia This Week
stories.headline_kid: A Singaporean man and his girlfriend were kidnapped in Malaysia and rescued by police, the second such rescue in just one week.
summary: A Singaporean man, who had entered Malaysia illegally in May, and his girlfriend, who entered legally, were kidnapped in Johor Bahru. The kidnappers demanded a ransom — money paid to free someone who has been captured — of about US$62,500, which is around S$85,000.
Thankfully, Malaysian police managed to rescue both of them safely. This is not the only case this week; another Singaporean was rescued from a similar kidnapping just days earlier.
These cases show that criminal gangs in the region are specifically targeting Singaporeans for ransom money. Police in both countries are working together to catch the culprits behind these crimes.
While kidnappings like this are rare, they remind us why it's important to stay cautious when travelling, avoid risky situations, and always let someone know your whereabouts.

lenses.me: It's a reminder to always tell a trusted adult where you're going, even on a short trip.
lenses.family: Families travelling to Malaysia may want to take extra safety precautions and stay in touch regularly.
lenses.friends: You and your friends can discuss why travel safety matters, even for short trips across the border.
lenses.nation: Singapore and Malaysian police are cooperating closely to protect citizens from cross-border crime.
lenses.world: It highlights how criminal networks can operate across country borders, targeting people from wealthier nations.

stories.title: Old Housing Estates Could Get a Brand New Life
stories.headline_kid: New rules might help old housing estates get sold together and rebuilt into bigger, newer homes.
summary: Long ago, the government built special housing estates called HUDC estates for middle-income families. Over time, many of these were sold to private owners, and now some are quite old, sitting on land with a 99-year lease — like a very long-term rental agreement with the government.

These estates are now around halfway through their lease. New proposed rules could make it easier for all the owners in an estate to agree to sell the whole place together to a developer. This is called an 'en bloc sale' — imagine everyone in your block of flats agreeing to sell together so a company can knock it down and build a bigger, modern building.

Because these estates have large plots of land, redeveloping them could create many more new homes than exist today. This is exciting news for people who might get a good payout from selling, and for future families who need housing.
However, en bloc sales can take a long time and require agreement from a majority of owners, so it's not guaranteed to happen quickly.

lenses.me: If you live in an older estate, your neighbourhood might change completely in the coming years.
lenses.family: Families who own flats in these estates could receive money from a sale, but might also need to find a new home.
lenses.friends: Friends living in these areas might move away if their estate is redeveloped, changing your friend group.
lenses.nation: Singapore has limited land, so reusing old estates helps create more homes for a growing population.
lenses.world: Many crowded cities around the world face similar challenges of rebuilding old areas to fit more people.

stories.title: From Coding to Cooking: Why This Man Chose Hokkien Mee Over a Big Tech Job
stories.headline_kid: A man who earned S$10,000 a month at a tech job now sells Hokkien mee at a hawker stall, working harder for less pay but loving it more.
summary: Alvin Tan, 30, used to work in the technology industry and earned a comfortable salary of S$10,000 a month. But instead of waiting to see if his company would let him go, called retrenchment, he decided to leave on his own terms.

Alvin took a big leap and opened a hawker stall selling Hokkien mee, a popular Singapore noodle dish. Running a hawker stall means very long hours — often much longer than an office job — and he now earns far less money than before.

Despite this, Alvin says he feels happier because he has more control over his future and enjoys the work he does every day. His story raises an interesting question: is it worth giving up money and comfort to do something you truly enjoy?

Hawker food is a treasured part of Singapore's culture, recognised by UNESCO as an important heritage. Stories like Alvin's show how some Singaporeans are choosing passion over pay, keeping this tradition alive.

lenses.me: It makes you think about what matters more to you — earning a lot of money or doing something you truly enjoy.
lenses.family: Families sometimes have different opinions on whether to choose a stable job or follow a passion — this could spark a good dinner conversation.
lenses.friends: You and your friends might enjoy discussing what kind of job you'd want when you grow up.
lenses.nation: Hawker food is part of Singapore's identity, and stories like this help keep the tradition alive for the next generation.
lenses.world: Around the world, more people are rethinking whether high salaries are worth long hours and stress, choosing meaningful work instead.
